title: Orders API Database Connection Pool Exhaustion
executive_summary: A routine deployment introduced a database query missing a required index, which under normal traffic exhausted the connection pool for the orders database. This caused checkout and order-history failures for roughly 80% of active users for approximately 93 minutes, resolved by rolling back the deployment.
timeline_summary: 14:10 - orders-api v2.14.0 deployed with new unindexed query
14:22 - Connection pool utilization warning alert fires
14:30 - Connection pool utilization critical alert fires
14:32 - On-call SRE paged as checkout begins returning 500 errors
14:52 - Root cause identified: full table scans from missing index
15:12 - Connection pool and latency return to baseline

root_cause_analysis.trigger: Deployment of orders-api v2.14.0 introducing a new /orders/history query path.
root_cause_analysis.root_cause: Schema/query review process for the new deploy did not include a query-plan (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) check, so a query without a supporting index reached production.
five_whys: Why did users see 500 errors? Because the API could not obtain a database connection.
Why couldn't it get a connection? Because the connection pool was exhausted.
Why was the pool exhausted? Because queries were taking far longer than normal, holding connections open.
Why were queries slow? Because a newly deployed query was performing a full table scan on the orders table.
Why did it perform a full table scan? Because there was no index on orders.customer_id supporting the new query.
Why was the index missing? Because code review for the new endpoint did not include a query-plan check as part of the merge checklist.
contributing_factors: No automated query-plan linting in CI for new database access code
Connection pool had no hard ceiling/alerting margin between warning (80%) and critical (100%) thresholds, leaving little response buffer
No canary/staged rollout for orders-api; v2.14.0 went to 100% of traffic immediately

what_went_well: On-call SRE acknowledged the page within 3 minutes and declared the incident within 5 minutes of detection
Database SME correctly identified the full table scan via slow query logs within 16 minutes of investigation starting
IC chose rollback over a risky live index build under load, restoring service in 36 minutes
Status page was updated within the SEV1 15-minute communication window at each phase
what_went_wrong: The unindexed query was not caught in code review or CI before reaching production
No canary/staged rollout meant 100% of traffic was exposed immediately
Alerting thresholds (80% warning, 100% critical) left minimal buffer to react before user-facing impact began
Customer-facing communication described impact as 'a subset of users' when actual impact was approximately 80%

action_items.description: Add automated EXPLAIN ANALYZE / query-plan check to CI for any PR modifying database access code touching the orders table.
Add missing index on orders.customer_id supporting the /orders/history query path.
Introduce staged/canary rollout (10% -> 50% -> 100%) for orders-api deployments.
Lower connection pool warning threshold to 60% and add a mid-tier 'elevated' alert to widen the reaction window.
Update customer communication guidelines to require an impact-percentage estimate (even rough) in the first status page update for SEV1/SEV2 incidents.

lessons_learned: Traffic-triggered failures often expose a latent design gap rather than being caused by the traffic itself; the connection pool had no headroom to absorb an unexpected latency increase from any source. Query-plan review needs to be enforced by tooling, not just review diligence, and rollout strategy should assume any single deploy can be the root cause until ruled out.
